alignment.note: Both Greek and Vulgate open the sentence with the connective καί / Et, which the Peshitta omits, beginning instead directly with the verb ܐܡܪ; asyndeton is a common feature of Syriac narrative style.
εἶπεν αὐτοῖς / ܐܡܪ ܠܗܘܢ / dixit illis; the Vulgate adds an editorial colon (idx 3) introducing direct discourse, a punctuation feature absent in the source traditions.
τὸ γένος / ܓܢܣܐ / genus; the Greek articular noun is matched by the emphatic-state Syriac form and the anarthrous Latin, all denoting 'this kind' of demon.

ἐν οὐδενί / in nullo render 'by nothing' with preposition plus indefinite; Syriac ܒܡܕܡ ('by anything') combined with the following negative ܠܐ achieves the same negative-instrumental sense by a different syntactic distribution.

δύναται / potest is a single positive verb; the Syriac expresses the negated modal as ܠܐ ܡܫܟܚ ('is not able'), splitting the negation across two tokens (idx 5–6) where Greek and Latin locate the negation earlier in οὐδενί / nullo.
The Greek conditional idiom εἰ μή ('except') is rendered by the single Syriac particle ܐܠܐ and the Latin nisi, all functioning as the exceptive marker.

Greek and Latin list 'prayer and fasting' (προσευχῇ καὶ νηστείᾳ / oratione et jejunio), whereas the Peshitta inverts the pair to 'fasting and prayer' (ܒܨܘܡܐ ܘܒܨܠܘܬܐ); the reversed order is a recurrent Syriac liturgical convention. Note also that several Greek witnesses omit καὶ νηστείᾳ altogether, a variant not reflected here.
